amendments.rule: The **substantival article** — `הַ` on a participle or adjective used as a noun — takes the pronoun the ASV supplies to make it substantival, and heads on that pronoun rather than on the relative that follows it. `הָרַע` → *that which was evil* is the article with *that which*, headed on *that*; `הָעֹשֶׂה` → *him that doeth* is the article with *him that*, headed on *him*. The supplied pronoun is the article's own rendering and is never `added`. The predicate word keeps its own English, including any copula the ASV supplies, which stays with it under rule 20: in *that which is right*, *is* and *right* belong to the adjective and only *that which* belongs to the article. **An attributive article the ASV renders by a relative goes the same way.** Where `הַ` stands on a participle or adjective modifying an explicit noun and the ASV writes a relative instead of a *the* — `אֹיְבֶיךָ הַקָּמִים עָלֶיךָ` → *thine enemies that rise up against thee*, `הָאִישׁ הָרַךְ` → *The man that is tender*, `הַכְּתוּבִים` → *that are written*, `הַכֹּהֵן הַמְחַטֵּא` → *The priest that offereth* — the article takes that relative and heads on it, while the participle or adjective keeps its own English together with any supplied copula, exactly as above. **But read where the ASV has put the attributive before reaching for that sentence.** Where it renders the attributive prenominally instead, no relative stands before the attributive's own word and rule 47 governs the count: the phrase's single *the* is the first article's and the agreement article is `unrepresented`, as `הַכֹּהֵן הַמָּשִׁיחַ` → *the anointed priest* is. **A demonstrative, possessive or quantifying determiner the ASV writes in the article's place goes the same way, whatever the article stands on.** Where the ASV writes no *the* for the phrase but a *this*, *that*, *these*, *those*, a possessive *his*, *her*, *thy*, *thine*, or a quantifier such as *any* or *every*, standing where the phrase's *the* would stand — `הַזִּמָּה` → *this lewdness*, `הַגְּדֹלוֹת` → *thine elder*, `הַבֶּגֶד` → *any garment* — that word is what the ASV has written for the article: the article takes it and heads on it, and it is neither `added` nor a reason to mark the article `unrepresented`. A quantifying determiner is read on exactly the terms of the others and is not left to the noun under rule 15: that rule gives a supplied *any* to the nominal expression only where no determiner morpheme stands before the word it determines, and an article standing on that word is such a morpheme. **Read that as no *the* standing before the article's own word, not as no *the* anywhere in the phrase.** Where the article sits on the *nomen rectum* of a construct chain and the ASV writes a *the* before the construct and a demonstrative or possessive before the rectum's own word, rule 29's arthrous case governs the count: nothing is fronted, the article takes the determiner standing before its own word, and the construct takes the supplied *the*. `יְמֵי הַמִּשְׁתֶּה` → *the days of* ***their*** *feasting* gives *their* to the article and *the days* to the construct, exactly as `שְׂדֵה הָעִיר` → *the fields of the city* gives the second *the* to the article there. Do not mark such an article `unrepresented` and the determiner `added` under rule 18's closing sentence: that sentence governs a supplied possessive with no determiner morpheme standing before the word it determines, and here one does. **But only where no other morpheme licenses that determiner.** A pronominal suffix standing in the same phrase is rendered by a possessive of its own under rule 18, and a `כֹּל` standing on the noun is itself what an *any* or an *every* renders under rule 15; where the ASV writes one determiner for the whole phrase that morpheme takes it and the article is `unrepresented`: `אֲחוֹתֵךְ הַגְּדוֹלָה` → *thine elder sister* gives *thine* to the suffix on `אָחוֹת` and leaves the article nothing, while `אֲחוֹתַיִךְ הַגְּדֹלוֹת` → *thy sisters, thine elder sisters* writes a determiner for each and the article takes the second; so too `אֲחִיהֶם הַבְּכוֹר` → *their eldest brother's*, where the suffix takes *their* and the article has nothing. Count the determiners and read which word each stands before, as rule 29 counts the ASV's *the*s. Read what the ASV writes for the article and let that decide which rule governs: a bare *the* is rule 15's ordinary attributive article, a relative or a supplied pronoun is this rule's, a demonstrative, possessive or quantifying determiner is this rule's too, and where the ASV writes none of them the article is `unrepresented` under rule 29. Where coordinated attributives share a single written relative, the first article takes it and the rest are `unrepresented` under rules 22 and 47. **An articleless attributive that the ASV recasts as a relative clause keeps the supplied relative with the attributive itself.** Where an adjective or participle without an article modifies an explicit noun and the ASV writes a relative frame — `אֲדָמָה טְמֵאָה` → *a land that is unclean* — the attributive takes the relative together with its own English and any copula rule 20 supplies, headed on the word carrying its lexeme. The relative realizes the Hebrew attributive relation and is not `added`; rule 55's supplied clause subordinator is a different construction.
amendments.why: LEV.6.27 `הַבֶּגֶד` → *any garment* met a case rule 41's enumeration did not consider. As the rule stood, its closing sentence ('where the ASV writes none of them the article is `unrepresented`') sends a reader to mark the article unrepresented, while rule 15's *any* clause would hand the word to the noun — but rule 15 already limits itself to a bare noun with no determiner morpheme of its own, so with an article present neither rule places the word. The corpus carries the widening: it aligns `הַ` to *every*, headed on *every*, in 7 units, alongside *this*, *those*, *their*, *his*, *her*, *thy* and *what*, and shows no unit where a determiner standing before the article's own word goes elsewhere. Two smaller repairs travel with it: the `כֹּל` limiter, so that rule 15's `כָּל־עֵץ` → *any tree* is not overridden by an article elsewhere in the phrase, and a sentence marking the boundary with rule 47 that LEV.6.22 and LEV.6.26 turn on — a prenominally rendered attributive leaves the article an agreement article, not a relative-bearing one. Nothing else in the rule is altered.

conventions: The superlative construct קֹדֶשׁ קָדָשִׁים is split rather than fused: the rectum takes the ASV's 'most' under rule 19, the construct takes 'holy' together with the verbless clause's construction-supplied copula under rule 20, and an explicit הִוא standing in the clause takes only its own 'it'. Applied at LEV.6.17, 6.25 and 6.29. It is not read as one noncompositional unit, because rule 2 prefers the split wherever each member holds an English word of its own.

אִשֶּׁה is rendered by the phrase 'offerings made by fire' and heads on 'offerings', the noun the phrase turns on by rule 31's subtraction; 'fire' was the competing head. The unit is discontinuous where the ASV splits 'made by fire' off across the divine name (LEV.6.18) and continuous at LEV.6.17.

Where the ASV writes a noun's lexeme inside the following cognate verb's rendering, the noun takes only the pro-form the ASV writes for it and is `unrepresented` where none is written, while the lexeme stays with the verb: הָעֹשֶׁק אֲשֶׁר עָשָׁק -> 'the thing which he hath gotten by oppression' gives 'thing' to the noun, and הַגְּזֵלָה אֲשֶׁר גָּזָל -> 'that which he took by robbery' leaves the noun nothing, the article taking the demonstrative 'that' under rule 41. Both at LEV.6.4. BSB attaches the lexeme to the noun in the second case; that is the documented convention difference and not an error.

For הַכֹּהֵן + an articled attributive, read where the ASV has put the attributive. Rendered postnominally as a relative clause, its article takes the 'that' under rule 41 and the first article takes the single written 'the' (LEV.6.26, הַמְחַטֵּא -> 'The priest that offereth it for sin'). Rendered prenominally, rule 47 governs the count: the first article takes the 'the' and the agreement article is `unrepresented` (LEV.6.22, הַמָּשִׁיחַ -> 'the anointed priest'), and the relative the ASV then supplies for the following prepositional predicate תַּחְתָּיו is `added` under rule 55. The competing reading gives that relative to תַּחְתָּיו's own unit, alongside the copula rule 49 already puts there, on the analogy of rule 41's articleless attributive; it is named here because the contract's articleless-attributive clause reaches an adjective or participle and not a prepositional phrase.

report: Checked all 59 candidate groups plus the dump read end to end for added-side splits, which the lemma table cannot see. No construction is analysed two ways without something in the source or in the ASV licensing the difference, so patches is empty.

Cleared as ASV-driven rather than split: אֶחָד (any at 6.3, nothing at 6.7 where 'concerning whatsoever' swallows עַל אַחַת מִכֹּל); כֹּל (all / any thing / Every / fused with לֹא into 'no' at 6.30 against a separately written 'not' at 6.23); בְּ, עַל, מִן, לְ throughout; אָכַל, שָׁחַט, קָטַר, נָגַע, בּוֹא; and the four identical speech formulas at 6.1, 6.8, 6.19, 6.24.

Two near-splits examined closely and cleared. (a) 6.22 הַכֹּהֵן הַמָּשִׁיחַ -> 'the anointed priest that shall be in his stead' against 6.26 הַכֹּהֵן הַמְחַטֵּא -> 'The priest that offereth': the attributive is rendered prenominally in the first, so rule 47 gives the phrase's single 'the' to the first article and leaves the agreement article unrepresented, while in the second it is rendered postnominally as a relative clause, so rule 41 gives the 'that' to the attributive's article. (b) 6.4's four noun+relative+verb phrases are treated alike: the noun takes whatever pro-form the ASV writes for it ('the thing') and is unrepresented where none is written (הַגְּזֵלָה), the lexeme staying inside the verb's rendering.

The four added units are mutually consistent: 'his' at 6.10 t011 and 6.18 t013 are supplied where the Hebrew writes no suffix (every other possessive and object pronoun in the chapter answers to a written suffix), 'it' at 6.15 t035 is supplied where no object morpheme stands (each parallel eat/bring/offer clause does have one), and 'that' at 6.22 t005 is the chapter's only supplied subordinator.

BSB: none of the 24 disagreements is an error. The R x 11, Td x 4 and Sp3ms x 4 recurrences are the documented convention difference, where rules 16, 27, 29, 40, 47 and 52 leave a morpheme unrepresented and BSB attaches it to its phrase. The four singletons are convention too: גְּזֵלָה 6.4 and אַחַת 6.7 are lexemes the ASV writes once inside a neighbouring rendering, הִוא 6.9 is pleonastic before the repeated הָעֹלָה and gets no English at all, and אֹתָה 6.14 is an ordinary rule 16 object marker. Nothing was changed to move the 94.7% figure.

One edge I would revisit and did not patch: LEV.6.12's six-morpheme unit for בַּבֹּקֶר בַּבֹּקֶר -> 'every morning'. Rule 30's condition is one English rendering of which no morpheme owns a part, and 'morning' is spent on בֹּקֶר in particular, so the fusion is not licensed as written; the verse's stated reason for rejecting the split, that then no morpheme carries 'every', overlooks that the second occurrence is what the distributive English renders. It is a single-verse judgment whose competing reading is already recorded, and the contract does not clearly settle which morpheme takes 'every', so I left the accepted edge standing and flag it here instead.

Four conventions recorded, none of them a restatement: the superlative construct split, the אִשֶּׁה phrase and its head, the cognate-noun rule the ASV forces at 6.4, and the 6.22/6.26 attributive-article boundary with its competing reading named. One amendment to rule 41, widening the determiner sentence to a quantifier standing in the article's place.
